strengths: Well-motivated core idea: decomposing each LoRA rank-r update into r independent rank-one experts and using the learned key vector A_i itself as a self-activation signal, eliminating the need for a separately trained router. This is a natural and parameter-efficient extension of the associative-memory view of LoRA, and the ablation in Table 4 convincingly shows self-activation matches or beats an explicitly trained fine-grained router while saving 1.5x parameters.

Extensive and diverse empirical validation spanning CLIP continual learning (X-TAIL, MTIL, multiple task orders), T5-large and LLaMA2-7B text-classification CL benchmarks (both standard 4-5 task and extended 15-task sequences), and a dedicated study of forgetting/generalization on unseen domains (HumanEval/MMLU) with Llama-3.1-8B fine-tuning. Consistent and often substantial improvements over strong, recent baselines (MoE-Adapter, RAIL-Primal, CoDyRA, O-LoRA, LB-CL) across nearly all settings.

Thorough ablations isolating the contributions of top-k rank selection, temperature-based sharpness control, and test-time thresholding (Table 4, Fig. 4), plus a parameter/GPU-memory accounting (Tables 10, 15) showing MoRA activates far fewer parameters per task than baselines while achieving better performance.

Qualitative rank-activation visualizations (Fig. 3, 5, 6) and cumulative-activation statistics (Fig. 7-9) provide interpretable evidence for the claimed mechanisms of specialization, knowledge reuse, and reduced interference, going beyond aggregate accuracy numbers.
Reasonable reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, task orderings, and dataset descriptions are provided in the appendix, and code release is promised.
weaknesses: The 'linear associative memory' framing (Sec. 3.2, Eqs. 2-6) is presented as a theoretical grounding but is largely a descriptive analogy rather than a rigorous derivation; the leap from this framing to justifying that A_i x is a good relevance/self-activation score (Eq. 8) is not formally established, and the main support for the design remains empirical (Table 4) rather than theoretical.

As tasks accumulate, the total rank pool r_t grows linearly (e.g., up to ~176 ranks for 11-task MTIL), and the self-activation score in Eq. 8 requires normalization/top-k over all accumulated ranks at every forward pass; the paper does not discuss how this scales to substantially longer task sequences (hundreds of tasks) in terms of memory footprint or per-step routing computation, despite claiming 'little-by-little' incremental growth as a selling point.

Parameter/model growth is linear in the number of tasks (frozen ranks are never merged or compressed), which is a standard limitation of expansion-based CL approaches but is not explicitly discussed as a limitation, nor compared quantitatively against non-expanding baselines for very long streams.

Key hyperparameters (temperature τ_MoRA, activation budget k, threshold δ) are manually tuned per experiment/architecture (the paper notes 'optimal temperature can differ across models'), and no principled or automatic method for setting these is provided, which may hinder practical adoption; the future-work section acknowledges this but does not attempt it.

Statistical robustness (mean/std over multiple runs) is only reported for the CLIP X-TAIL experiments (Table 13); the LM continual-learning and generalization/forgetting results (Tables 2, 3, 8, 9) are reported as single-run numbers, leaving open questions about variance, especially given the fairly small margins over strong baselines like O-LoRA and LB-CL in some orderings.

The core novelty (rank-wise/rank-one expert decomposition with importance-based gating) has conceptual overlap with prior rank-importance methods (e.g., AdaLoRA-style singular value gating, MiLoRA) and other MoE-LoRA works; while the self-activation-without-separate-router mechanism and its application to CL forgetting mitigation is a meaningful contribution, the paper could more clearly delineate its incremental novelty relative to this broader rank-selection literature beyond the experimental comparisons already given.

strengths: Extensive experimental validation across three distinct settings (CLIP continual learning on X-TAIL/MTIL, LM continual learning on T5-large/LLaMA2-7B across multiple task orderings, and generalization/forgetting analysis with Llama-3.1-8B), which is broader than most competing papers in this space.

The associative-memory (key-value) reinterpretation of LoRA updates provides an intuitive conceptual lens connecting rank-one decomposition to interpretable specialization, and the accompanying activation visualizations (Figs. 3, 5, 6) offer some qualitative evidence for rank specialization and reduced interference.
Reasonably thorough ablation studies (Table 4, Fig. 4) isolating the contributions of self-activation, top-k masking, temperature sharpening, and test-time thresholding.

Reports parameter/GPU-memory efficiency comparisons (Tables 10, 15) and includes some robustness/variance results (Table 13) and additional benchmark comparisons in the appendix (HumanEval Pass@k, X-TAIL Order 2).
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is thin: 'self-activation' simply reuses the existing A matrix's projection as a relevance score, which is a fairly direct consequence of decomposing LoRA into rank-one terms; the paper largely combines well-known techniques (top-k gating, temperature-scaled softmax, thresholding) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism. The 'no external router' framing is somewhat oversold since A is itself a trained routing matrix.

Performance gains over the strongest baselines (e.g., CoDyRA, O-LoRA, LB-CL) are frequently modest (e.g., 71.3\%\to72.7\% Average in Table 1, 76.7\%\to77.6\% in Table 3), and most main tables lack error bars/statistical testing, making it hard to judge significance despite the partial variance results relegated to the appendix.

Key hyperparameters (temperature \tau_{MoRA}, threshold \delta, rank activation budget k) require per-architecture/per-task tuning, and the paper explicitly notes 'the optimal temperature setting can differ across pre-trained models,' undermining claims of a simple, broadly applicable self-activated design and raising reproducibility/generalization concerns.

No analysis of inference-time computational overhead as the accumulated rank pool grows across many tasks (e.g., scoring/top-k selection over hundreds of ranks per token per layer in long-sequence settings); only parameter counts and one-shot GPU memory are reported, leaving a gap in understanding scalability to long task streams.

Lack of load-balancing raises the possibility of rank underutilization or 'dead' experts over long sequences; while cumulative-activation statistics (Figs. 7-9) are shown, they do not directly address whether some ranks become permanently inactive or whether specialization is stable across many more than 10 tasks.

The associative-memory justification for why raw dot-product scores yield stable, non-redundant specialization (without any regularization enforcing orthogonality or diversity across ranks) is more of a plausible narrative than a rigorously established theoretical result.

Presentation is dense in places (e.g., Fig. 1/2, heavy notation in Sec. 3.2-3.4) and the very large number of baselines and tables can make it difficult to identify the decisive comparisons driving the paper's claims.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated core idea: decomposing LoRA rank-r updates into rank-one 'experts' and having each rank self-infer its own relevance (using its own key vector A_i as router) rather than relying on a separately trained router. This elegantly addresses the coarse-granularity, interference, and routing-ambiguity issues identified in existing MoE-LoRA approaches for continual learning.

The associative-memory view of LoRA (rank-1 components as key-value memory slots) offers an intuitive and reasonably principled justification for the self-activation mechanism, connecting to established literature on linear associative memories.

Extremely comprehensive empirical evaluation: CLIP continual learning on both X-TAIL and MTIL benchmarks, LM continual learning with T5-large and LLaMA2-7B across multiple task orderings (including long 15-task sequences), and a separate study of forgetting/generalization on Llama-3.1-8B via HumanEval and MMLU subjects.

Thorough ablation studies (Table 4, Fig. 4) that isolate the contribution of each design component (self-activation vs. learned router, top-k selection, temperature sharpness, test-time thresholding), providing good evidence for the individual mechanisms rather than only reporting an end-to-end number.

Strong and mostly consistent empirical gains over relevant, fairly recent baselines (MoE-Adapter, RAIL-Primal, CoDyRA, O-LoRA, LB-CL, InfLoRA, LoRI) across nearly all reported settings, including favorable parameter/memory efficiency (Tables 10, 15) and multiple-run variance analysis (Table 13) supporting robustness.

Interpretability analysis via rank activation visualizations (Fig. 3, 5, 6) and statistical sparsity analysis (Figs. 7-9) that supports the paper's mechanistic claims (specialization, knowledge reuse, reduced interference) rather than relying purely on aggregate accuracy numbers.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility information in the appendix (hyperparameters, task orderings, prompts, dataset details) and a stated intent to release code.
weaknesses: The associative-memory framing, while intuitive, is somewhat loosely connected to the actual algorithmic contribution (which is essentially a normalized/temperature-scaled/top-k-masked self-gating scheme); the 'memory' narrative reads partly as post-hoc motivation rather than a derivation that yields specific, non-obvious design choices.

The self-activation score computation (Eq. 8) normalizes over all accumulated ranks r_t, which grows linearly with the number of tasks; the paper does not clearly analyze or discuss the computational/inference cost implications of this at scale for very long task sequences, beyond a snapshot of parameter/memory counts at fixed task counts.

Key hyperparameters (temperature τ_MoRA, threshold δ, rank activation budget k) appear to require per-model/per-dataset tuning (the paper itself notes 'the optimal temperature setting can differ across each pre-trained model'), which raises concerns about ease of deployment and sensitivity, though ablations are provided for these choices.

Some claims are supported by a single ablation configuration (e.g., 'self-activation matches or surpasses a separately learned router' is shown only in one controlled setup in Table 4), limiting generality of that specific claim.

The method's growing pool of frozen ranks across tasks (memory grows with T) is not directly contrasted against baselines' growth rates in terms of long-term scalability/inference latency, only static per-task parameter counts and one memory snapshot are given.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy in the methodology section, which could be streamlined; some repeated/overlapping explanations (e.g., of associative memory and LoRA-as-memory) could be condensed to make room for deeper discussion of limitations or failure cases.

No theoretical guarantee or bound on forgetting is provided; contribution is primarily empirical/mechanistic rather than establishing formal guarantees, though this is a reasonable scope limitation rather than a flaw given the empirical thoroughness.

strengths: The paper is well-motivated: it precisely diagnoses coarse-grained expert/routing problems in existing MoE-LoRA continual learning methods (interference, redundancy, routing collapse) and proposes a conceptually clean fix by decomposing rank-r LoRA updates into rank-1 atomic units.

The self-activation mechanism (deriving mixture weights directly from the intrinsic key vectors instead of training an external router) is a practical, parameter-free simplification that plausibly reduces one source of instability (router drift) as the expert pool grows, and the paper empirically supports this claim via a routing-strategy ablation (Table 4) showing self-activated retrieval avoids the 'retrieval collapse' seen with an external router over many fine-grained atoms.

Extensive empirical coverage: experiments span vision-language CLIP continual learning (X-TAIL, MTIL, multiple orderings), several LLM backbones (LLaMA-2/3, Gemma) on TRACE and standard/long-sequence LM classification benchmarks, and a standard fine-tuning forgetting/generalization study on code + MMLU subjects, providing a fairly broad basis for the claims.

Reasonably thorough ablations and analyses: component-wise ablation of routing strategies (Table 4), sensitivity sweeps over activation budget, temperature, and threshold (Fig. 4), order-robustness (OPD-style) analysis (Table 14), parameter/GPU-memory accounting (Tables 11, 18), and a post-pruning study showing atoms can be compacted with minor performance loss (Table 19).

Qualitative visualizations of rank activations (Fig. 3, 6, 7) provide interpretable evidence for the intended mechanism: individual ranks specializing on semantic patches and being reused/preserved across tasks, which supports (though does not rigorously prove) the forgetting-mitigation narrative.

Method is efficient in trainable/activated parameters relative to several baselines (Table 11, 18), and improvements hold with a favorable stability-plasticity trade-off in several benchmarks (e.g., TRACE OP/BWT in Table 2, SuperNI results in Table 13).
weaknesses: The core theoretical framing (Definition 1, 'Weight Matrix as Linear Associative Memory') largely restates the elementary fact that any rank-r matrix is a sum of r rank-1 outer products; casting this in memory/key-value terminology is evocative but does not add rigorous new theory (e.g., no analysis of interference bounds, capacity, or orthogonality conditions typically central to associative memory models), so the framing risks overstating novelty relative to prior fine-grained MoE/rank-1 expert work (e.g., DeepSeekMoE, Mixture of a Million Experts, MoLE) that is cited but not clearly differentiated at a mechanistic level.

Reported gains over the strongest baseline (CoDyRA) are often modest and not always consistent: e.g., in Table 1 Transfer scores are nearly tied (63.30 vs 63.2), and CoDyRA outperforms MoRAM on several individual columns (e.g., Food, OxfordPet 'Last'); most main results tables (Table 1, 12, 17) do not report variance across runs, making it hard to judge whether the improvements are statistically meaningful (only Tables 2, 16 provide standard deviations).

Memory grows linearly with the number of tasks (r new atoms per task) since old atoms are always frozen and retained; while a post-hoc pruning analysis is presented (Table 19, ~30% reduction), it is not integrated into most main experiments and its effect on longer task streams (beyond ~15 tasks) is untested, leaving scalability to many more tasks an open question.

Several key hyperparameters (temperature τ_MoRAM, threshold δ, rank activation budget k) differ substantially across settings (e.g., τ=0.5 for code fine-tuning vs. 0.03 for TRACE vs. 0.1 for CLIP), suggesting the 'no extra regularization needed' simplicity claim understates the practical tuning burden and the method's sensitivity to these knobs across architectures/domains is not systematically studied outside the CLIP ablation.

The self-activation relevance score (Eq. 5) requires normalizing over all accumulated rt atoms for every input, and how this scales computationally (latency, memory) as rt grows over long task sequences is not empirically benchmarked (only parameter counts and training-time GPU memory are reported, not inference cost trends with t).

The paper offers largely empirical/heuristic justifications ('we believe', 'we empirically observe') for design choices such as omitting load-balancing regularization, without theoretical grounding for why fine-grained rank-1 experts naturally avoid the load-imbalance and dead-expert problems well documented in the MoE literature.

Limitations discussion in the main text is brief and generic (future work paragraph), without deeper engagement with failure modes such as tasks requiring shared high-rank structure that cannot be well approximated by sparse rank-1 combinations, or scenarios where fine-grained specialization could hurt positive transfer.
